reason: While the text describes specific practices that could be classified as rituals (daily manna gathering and Shabbat observance), the primary emphasis is not on rituals and ceremonies as important in themselves. Instead, the text stresses obedience to God's commandments and Torah (instructions). Key phrases reveal this: Yahweh tests whether the people will 'walk in my Torah' (לְמַעַן אֲנַסֶּנּוּ הֲיֵלֵךְ בְּתוֹרָתִי), and God questions 'how long will you refuse to keep my commandments and teachings' (עַד־ אָנָה מֵֽאַנְתֶּם לִשְׁמֹר מִצְוֺתַי וְתוֹרֹתָֽי). The rituals are presented as expressions of obedience to divine law, not as the fundamental object of God's concern. The text's framing emphasizes the relational and ethical dimension—whether the people will follow God's instruction—rather than the intrinsic importance of ritualistic practice.
